articles.body: CAIRO, July 25 (Reuters) - An Israeli airstrike on Saturday killed the head of the Hamas-led police force in the northern Gaza Strip, Brigadier-General Abdel-Nasser Al-Maqadma, the group-run interior ministry and ​medics said. Medics and the interior ministry said Maqadma, known also as the governor ‌of northern Gaza Strip, was killed by an Israeli airstrike in the Sheikh Radwan area north of Gaza City. The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up here. In a separate incident, another Israeli strike killed a Palestinian medic in the Nuseirat refugee camp in ​central Gaza Strip, medics said. They added that a police officer, wounded by an ​Israeli airstrike last week, died on Saturday. The Israeli military did not immediately ⁠comment on any of the incidents. Israel has killed dozens of members of the Hamas-led police force , opens new tab , ​including senior officials, in the past months, accusing many of them of being members of the ​Hamas armed wing who posed imminent threats to Israel and its forces inside Gaza. Hamas says Israeli attacks on the police force and its headquarters are intended to sow chaos and anarchy in the enclave and violate ​the U.S.-brokered October ceasefire . The latest deaths add to a toll of more than 1,180 Palestinians, mostly ​civilians, killed by Israeli attacks since an October ceasefire between Israel and Hamas militants took effect, according to ‌Gaza ⁠health officials. Hamas does not usually disclose its losses. The truce halted full-scale fighting but has not ended near-daily Israeli strikes. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period. Mediators including Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the United States have been trying to advance U.S. ​President Donald Trump's plan ​for ending the ⁠conflict in Gaza, which calls for Hamas disarmament and Israeli withdrawals, but there has been little sign of progress in the efforts. The war began ​when Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, killing 1,200 people and taking ​about 250 ⁠hostages, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent offensive has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, say Gaza health officials. Israel effectively controls an estimated 64% of the tiny coastal Strip, bombarded to ruins by Israel's ⁠two-year ​military assault that followed the 2023 Hamas attack on ​southern Israel. Nearly all of Gaza's 2 million people now live on a tiny strip of land, mainly in makeshift tents ​or damaged buildings and facing dire conditions , under Hamas control. articles.body: Summary Blazes moving inland towards France's ninth city Flames now 30 km from Bordeaux, suburbs cleared Of three fires near Madrid, two have merged Spain awaiting water-dumping aircraft from abroad Spanish minister warns against outside activity BORDEAUX, France/MADRID, July 25 (Reuters) - Wildfires on the coast of southwestern France moved inland towards Bordeaux on Saturday, forcing the evacuation of thousands in the ‌city's suburbs, while in neighbouring Spain high winds complicated efforts to fight a massive blaze near Madrid. Hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated in both countries because of those fires, the latest natural disasters linked to sustained dry spells and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Stay up to date on the key companies, data, and decisions in the ESG world with the Reuters Sustainable Finance newsletter. Sign up here. "The fires that ​are hitting our country have reached a level that has never been seen before," French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on ​X. "We expect a fight that will be long and very difficult," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez later told reporters, adding ⁠that Bordeaux airport had been closed. France's armed forces have been drafted in to help overwhelmed fire brigades, while Spain has declared its first national ​emergency over a wildfire, because of three blazes, two of which merged on Friday. Spain's Civil Protection Service said it was expecting four more ​water-dumping aircraft to arrive on Saturday, two from Italy and two from Greece - sent as part of a European Union response to the emergency. Firefighting aircraft from the Netherlands and Portugal have already been deployed in Spain. High winds have stoked and spread the fires in both countries. The coast near Bordeaux is a tourist hotspot which ​includes pine forests that can catch fire easily. The city is also famous for its eponymous wines, made by nearby vineyards. Roughly 197,000 people ​have so far been evacuated from the Gironde and Landes regions close to Bordeaux since the wildfires broke out there this week. More than 63,000 people ‌have been ⁠evacuated or confined to their homes in Spain because of the three major fires there. REUTERS/Ana Beltran Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab French Interior Minister Nunez said the fire was around 30 km (19 miles) from Bordeaux, adding that the situation was calmer on Saturday but that winds were expected to pick up again in the afternoon. The government has warned against road or rail travel to the area. SPAIN WARNS AGAINST GOING OUTSIDE Many Madrid residents have second homes in the densely ​populated area west of the capital ​but still in the region ⁠of Madrid where the two fires merged. A third fire in Avila province has threatened to merge with the two in Madrid, Nicanor Sen, the government representative for the Castile and Leon region, told reporters on Friday. Esteban ​Carrasco, owner of the Monasterio de Pelayos campsite west of the capital, told national broadcaster TVE about ​30 mobile homes ⁠were burned down when the fire reached the site on Friday. About 200 campers from "humble backgrounds" had to evacuate, he added. "It was a horrific disaster," he said as he showed how mobile homes on one side of a road were destroyed while on the other side they escaped untouched. No ⁠one was ​injured. While smoke filled the air in Madrid on Friday, it was clearer on Saturday ​but Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia still warned against outdoor activities. "Avoid physical activity and staying outdoors. If you go outdoors and there is smoke or ash, use a mask," she ​said on X. REUTERS/Mohammed Torokman [4/4] A general view of the village of Tal, near Nablus, the day after four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shooting incident near the village, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank,... Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab Read more Summary Netanyahu orders crackdown after West Bank shooting incident Palestinians say shootout provoked by armed settlers Social media footage shows confused confrontation RAMALLAH, July 25 (Reuters) - Israeli forces arrested dozens of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, after at least four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers ​were killed in a shootout when armed Israeli settlers approached a Palestinian village. Palestinian authorities in the West Bank said ‌Friday's shootings were provoked by the settlers who aimed to attack villagers in Tal, southwest of Nablus. The Israeli military initially described the Israeli civilians involved in the incident as hikers, but later acknowledged some were armed and said both sides had opened fire before troops intervened. The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up here. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to take "powerful ​action" in response to the incident, including demolishing the home of the family of one of the Palestinians involved. Netanyahu's ​office said he would accelerate the approval of construction of more Israeli settlements in the area. Walid Zidan, ⁠the mayor of Tal, said around 70 people from the village had been detained and questioned at a field interrogation centre set up ​in a house in the village. Around 10 to 12 had been released so far, he told Reuters by telephone. "House raids are continuing, ​army patrols are driving through the streets, and there is no movement of people in the streets," he said. Hundreds of thousands of Israeli settlers live among millions of Palestinians in the West Bank, which Israel captured in a war in 1967. Nearly all countries and UN bodies consider such settlements illegal under international ​law. Israel disputes this, citing biblical and historical ties to the land. Recent months have seen a sharp increase in attacks by Israeli settlers ​on Palestinian villages. Friday's incident took place in the so-called "area A" of the West Bank, where Palestinian authorities have administrative control and Israeli civilians are barred under ‌Israeli ⁠law from entering. Area A comprises less than a fifth of the West Bank. Footage circulating on social media of the incident that led to Friday's shootout appeared to show a confused standoff between a crowd of villagers and a large group of Israelis, at least some of them armed, with soldiers also visible. At one point, at least two Israelis are seen pushing and hitting Palestinians with the stocks of their ​rifles, before one of the Palestinians ​seizes one of the weapons ⁠and is then apparently shot dead. In the background, voices can be heard shouting in Hebrew "Get away," "He's trying to snatch his weapon. He's snatched his weapon," and "Shoot him!" A child's voice is heard shouting "Revenge!" Reuters has ​not been able to authenticate the footage independently. CONFRONTATION Israel's army chief Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir said the security ​operation launched after ⁠the shootings was intended "to thwart terrorism, ensure the security of Israeli civilians and prevent further escalation". Zidan, the mayor, said the incident had been triggered by Israeli settlers deliberately harassing the village. "The settlers were not following a route or trail, as they claim. They intended to attack the homes," ⁠Zidan said. "People ​did not go there looking for a confrontation with them; they were simply defending ​their homes, nothing more and nothing less." The sharp increase in settler attacks on Palestinian villages in the West Bank seen in recent months has drawn condemnation from international agencies and ​countries in Europe but has done little to reverse the trend. Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab Read more Summary Companies Russia's largest online retailer has suffered series of warehouse attacks Yekaterinburg is hosting Russian Athletics Championships Downed drone sparks fire in city parking lot, says governor YEKATERINBURG, Russia July 25 (Reuters) - A drone threat prompted leading Russian ​online retailer Wildberries to evacuate its logistics hub on Saturday in the city of ‌Yekaterinburg, where the national athletics championships were also briefly suspended. Ukraine has struck Wildberries' warehouses in a string of attacks over the past week, broadening its long-range drone strategy to target a company central to Russia's consumer economy. The Reuters Daily Briefing newsletter provides all the news you need to start your day. Sign up here. Wildberries said ​it had temporarily halted operations at the Yekaterinburg facility for security reasons, but that the ​site had not been damaged. Around four hours later, it said operations had ⁠resumed. Earlier on Saturday, local authorities declared a drone alert over the wider Sverdlovsk region and said ​one attack had been repelled over Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city. Falling drone debris set fire to a ​parking lot, Governor Denis Pasler wrote on the Telegram app. "Economic and infrastructure facilities were not damaged," he said, cautioning residents to remain vigilant as the drone threat persisted. The alert also delayed the penultimate day of competition at the ​Russian Athletics Championships, which the city was hosting. Athletes and spectators had to leave the open stadium ​and take shelter, according to a Reuters witness. "This has never happened to me at competitions, but in everyday life ‌it ⁠has. Sometimes, even during training, we'll have drone alerts and sirens going off. So, it's a normal atmosphere, so to speak," said runner Anastasia Fedonina from the southwestern Volgograd region. Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone attacks on Russian infrastructure this year in a bid to undermine its war effort and ​pressure the Kremlin to make ​peace. It says it ⁠has targeted Wildberries on the grounds that it handles military supplies, which the Kremlin has denied. Since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, ​Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukrainian logistics infrastructure, as well as its energy system ​and power ⁠grid. On Saturday, local authorities in Russia's southern Krasnodar region said open flames had been extinguished at a warehouse hit by drones on Wednesday. They did not name the facility, but a Wildberries warehouse in Krasnodar ⁠was ​attacked that day. Together with smaller rivals, Wildberries and top competitor ​Ozon sell goods and services worth the equivalent of 8.5% of Russia's gross domestic product and employ 4 million people, or ​more than 5% of the country's workforce. REUTERS/Ammar Awad Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab RAMALLAH, West Bank, July 25 (Reuters) - Palestinian officials welcomed UNESCO's designation of Sebastia in the occupied West Bank as a World Heritage site, hoping it will prevent Israel extending ​its control at the ancient village, while Israel condemned it as a political ‌decision. Sebastia, in the northern West Bank, has archaeological remnants from successive periods dating back at least to the 9th-century BC capital of the Israelite kingdom, through the Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic periods, Crusader and Ottoman ​eras, according to UNESCO, the United Nations cultural organisation. The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up here. Olive trees surround the site, dotting ​a landscape of Roman columns, ancient walls and stone steps and an ⁠amphitheatre. It is traditionally seen as the burial place of John the Baptist. But Palestinian residents ​of the adjacent village, many of whom rely on tourism for a living, are facing ​land confiscations after Israel announced a plan to seize about 1,800 dunams (445 acres) at the site, which it said was meant to develop the area. On Friday, UNESCO added Sebastia to its World Heritage List and to the ​List of World Heritage in Danger, a related mechanism used to flag listed heritage sites ​that are facing serious threats, to try and safeguard them. "We hope that this decision will enable us ‌to preserve ⁠Sebastia," said Nizar Kayed, the village deputy mayor. He said that Israel's land seizure decision, announced in late 2025, was part of an Israeli push to expand settlements in the area. The Palestinian tourism and foreign ministries said on Friday that they hoped the UNESCO recognition would ​help mobilize international support ​against Israeli measures ⁠there. Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the UNESCO decision was part of a Palestinian drive to obscure Jewish ties to the land. "No vote ​in an international organization can change history," he said in a statement. Palestinian ​officials are ⁠also concerned about a new Israeli bill , that has yet to be written into law, that would extend Israeli civil control over ancient sites in the West Bank. That in effect would strip away ⁠oversight of ​the ancient sites from the Western-backed Palestinian Authority, which ​under the 1990s Oslo peace accords has exercised limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, territory Israel captured ​in a 1967 war. articles.body: A cargo ship full of shipping containers is seen at the port of Oakland, California, U.S., August 4, 2025. REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab Summary New forced-labor duties of 10% or 12.5% cover 99.4% of U.S. imports, USTR said Greer said rebuilt tariff layers will not exceed caps in negotiated trade deals The latest actions include probes into excess capacity and alleged Vietnamese intellectual property theft WASHINGTON, July 25 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump had no time for lengthy tariff investigations when he returned to office last year, wanting to hammer trading partners right away to wring concessions. What followed was a chaotic start to a ​trade agenda that was eventually upended by a stinging Supreme Court defeat this year. Now he and his team are moving into a new phase to build a more durable U.S. tariff wall using ‌more traditional and court-tested trade laws, those he had little patience for 18 months ago. Jumpstart your morning with the latest legal news delivered straight to your inbox from The Daily Docket newsletter. Sign up here. His latest global tariff salvo — duties of 10% or 12.5% on 60 countries over allegedly weak enforcement of forced-labor bans — marks the first of numerous tariff actions to be unveiled in the months ahead. They include probes into excess industrial capacity, alleged intellectual property theft by Vietnam, and national security protections for strategic industries from semiconductors to robotics and industrial machinery. "We're at the end of the beginning of the Trump tariff agenda," said Dan Ujczo, associate general counsel at Canadian oil producer Cenovus ​Energy, who specializes in U.S.-Canada trade. "Within the next few weeks, and certainly by the end of the summer, we will see large parts of President Trump's trade policy fully in effect." This could bring more clarity and certainty ​for businesses on Trump's ultimate tariff structure, along with dread in foreign trade ministries that they may have to cough up more concessions to protect access to a $3.4 trillion U.S. ⁠import market. DIRECT REPLACEMENTS Trump's new anti-forced labor duties imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, the unfair trade practices statute used against China during his first term, almost directly replace a global 10% temporary tariff that expired on Friday. ​They cover 99.4% of U.S. imports, the U.S. Trade Representative's office said. This rebuilds part of Trump's signature "Liberation Day" tariffs of 10%-50% on nearly every country, which the U.S. Supreme Court struck down as illegal under an untested national emergencies law Trump used ​to impose them. Another part of the baseline tariffs is likely to be rebuilt by another Section 301 investigation into excess industrial capacity , targeting 16 big trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan, South Korea, Mexico and Vietnam. That ongoing probe targets industrial subsidies and other export-focused policies. Amid a wider uproar over Trump's move, some viewed it as largely maintaining the status quo. Mark Bissell, CEO of Michigan-based vacuum maker Bissell Inc, said the newest tariffs were largely what the company anticipated and it hadn`t frontloaded inventory from China and elsewhere to try to beat them. "We continued to run ​the business based on the belief that the tariffs would stay in the 10-15% range," Bissell said in an email to Reuters. BUDGET IMPACT Trump's gamble on quick but untested tariffs right out of the gate did four things. It heaped added costs ​onto retailers and other import-dependent industries; it brought dozens of trading partners to the negotiating table, yielding concessions for lower rates; it prompted swift retaliation and tariff escalation from China that led to a delicate truce; and it filled U.S. fiscal coffers with hundreds of ‌billions of dollars. ⁠The Liberation Day tariffs alone yielded $166 billion in revenue, a major offset to a growing federal deficit, but refunds to importers have now turned those collections negative. The 150-day temporary tariffs, based on a law meant to quell balance-of-payments crises, have added $31 billion in assessed revenue through July 5. But if a federal court ruling against them stands, that money, too, is subject to refund. With U.S. public debt approaching $40 trillion, Josh Lipsky, chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council, said subsequent administrations may become addicted to tariff revenue that is likely to be sustained. "The tariff wall is being rebuilt strong brick by strong brick, and it's very durable," Lipsky said. Trump's broad use of Section 301 in the forced-labor case prompted an immediate legal challenge by small businesses, but trade and ​legal experts say this will take time to play out. ​The statute has a solid track record in the ⁠courts, and judges may be reluctant to enjoin actions aimed at curbing forced labor and lowering barriers to U.S. goods. MORE TO COME U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer made clear this week that Trump will use everything at his disposal to erect tariffs to reshore production and shrink the trade deficit. "The specific authorities this administration is using have changed, but the trade strategy has not," ​Greer told the U.S. Senate Finance Committee. Greer, who has not committed to a timeline for the industrial capacity investigations, has said the layers of tariffs being rebuilt will not ​exceed caps included in deals he ⁠has been negotiating, including 15% for the EU, Japan and South Korea and higher rates for Southeast Asian countries. Administration officials say even though China is viewed as the world's largest source of excess manufacturing, its rates will not exceed the cap of about 20% agreed by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping last November, which is on top of the 25% tariffs from his first term. Some nominal — or announced — duties may be higher than actual applied rates, which analysts say may be an enforcement mechanism for countries to stick ⁠to agreed trade ​deal terms. Still, some things continue to come out of the blue, including the 50% duties on Canadian beer, dairy, hockey sticks and other products Trump ​announced on Monday over Ottawa's refusal to make trade concessions, and his threat to cut off all trade with Spain over not meeting NATO military spending targets. That proclivity for spontaneous tariff announcements remains an ongoing risk, said Eswar Prasad, a trade professor at Cornell University and former head of the International ​Monetary Fund's China department. "Trump`s eagerness to impose tariffs to address a whole range of grievances will not only continue disrupting the global trading system but will have significant adverse effects on American households and businesses." "We have done it," said Abhijeet Dipke , founder of the Cockroach Janta Party ​that led the protests, to loud cheers at the Jantar Mantar ⁠protest site in New Delhi. Make sense of global markets with the Trading Day newsletter. Sign up here. India's biggest street protests of recent years have become ​a political flashpoint, posing one of the biggest challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi ​as politicians joined youngsters' calls to demand action. "Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar (protest site) and across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation ... ​I have sent my resignation letter to the Prime Minister," Dharmendra Pradhan wrote in ​his post. "I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country's youth." The minister announced ‌his ⁠resignation on X just as police fired tear gas to scatter young protesters in New Delhi, hours before their leaders were set to hold another round of talks with ministers. Youngsters at the Jantar Mantar site shouted "Jai Hind", a patriotic slogan meaning "Victory to ​India". Thousands of supporters ​of India's youth-led "cockroach" ⁠movement had been protesting since June, but anger boiled over since police on Monday injured dozens of students, launching baton charges and ​firing tear gas to deter crowds of protesters marching on parliament. The ​protests, led ⁠largely by young people and triggered by discontent over leaks of question papers for high-stakes entrance exams, reflect anger over job scarcity, corruption and government accountability. Federal authorities even ⁠on Saturday ​restricted access to the internet and to 18 ​metro stations to try to limit the protest in the capital, the latest day of such restrictions. Purchase Licensing Rights , opens new tab Read more Summary Companies Guterres to meet Syrian president, address new parliament Visit to Syria is first for any UN chief since 2009 Damascus has been rebuilding global ties, including at UN BEIRUT, July 25 (Reuters) - U.N. ​Secretary General Antonio Guterres arrived in Damascus on Saturday for the first trip to Syria by a serving United Nations' chief ‌since 2009, before the start of a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. "The United Nations stands with Syria at this pivotal moment," Guterres said in a post on X on arriving for what he described as a "visit of solidarity". He appealed to the international community to "spare no effort" to support the Syrian people. The Reuters Iran Briefing newsletter keeps you informed with the latest developments and analysis of the Iran war. Sign up here. Syrian ​President Ahmed al Sharaa received Guterres at the presidential palace in Damascus, state news agency SANA said. Sharaa, the former head of al ​Qaeda's affiliate in Syria, was until November 2025 under terrorism-related sanctions imposed by the U.N. Security Council. Guterres' visit is ⁠another milestone for Syria since rebels ousted president Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, ending the war that began in 2011 and launching a transitional ​period steered by an Islamist-led leadership. At the time, Guterres described "the end of the Syrian dictatorship" under Assad as a sign of hope for the region. The ​U.N. chief will also meet Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, other government officials and representatives of Syrian civil society, U.N. spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said on Tuesday. SYRIA RETURNS TO GLOBAL STAGE Guterres will underline that the country has an opportunity "not only to recover from conflict, but also to lay the foundations for a future for Syria that will be more ​stable, more inclusive, and more prosperous for all Syrians," Dujarric said. Guterres is expected to be in Damascus for several days, but the full schedule ​of his visit has not been released by his office. He is visiting just weeks after two bombs exploded near a hotel in Damascus where French President Emmanuel Macron spent ‌the night, ⁠overshadowing the first visit to Syria by a European Union head of state since Assad was toppled. Sharaa's government is seeking to rebuild Syria's international ties and economy after nearly 14 years of war and decades of isolation under Assad family rule. The transition has been marred by two major episodes of sectarian bloodshed that have tested Sharaa's repeated pledges to protect Syria's religious minorities. Nearly 1,500 Alawites — the sect that Assad is from — were killed in Syria's ​coastal region last year by government-aligned factions, ​and hundreds of Syrians from ⁠the Druze minority were killed months later in the south. Guterres expressed alarm over both bouts of violence and has called for accountability. Sharaa, who broke ties with al Qaeda in 2016, led an alliance of Islamist rebel factions ​that ousted Assad in a lightning offensive in December 2024. Since taking power, his government has sought to re-establish ​Syria's diplomatic ties to ⁠expand beyond Assad's longtime allies, Russia and Iran . Last year, Sharaa became the first Syrian president since 1967 to take part in the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The United States has lifted most sweeping sanctions on Syria and U.S. President Donald Trump informed Sharaa earlier this month that he intended to remove Syria from ⁠Washington's list ​of state sponsors of terrorism . Guterres is expected to address Syria's new parliament on Monday and will ​visit a U.N. peacekeeping force that has maintained a buffer zone between Israeli and Syrian forces for decades, Dujarric said. Israeli troops have occupied new areas in southern Syria after Assad was ​ousted. Damascus has demanded they withdraw and return to a 1974 disengagement agreement. articles.body: McALLEN, Texas — Just miles from the U.S.-Mexico border, Ken Paxton is trying to inherit President Donald Trump’s historic gains with Hispanic voters. The Texas GOP Senate nominee, speaking to hundreds of supporters last week at his first campaign rally in this region that’s almost entirely Latino, revealed how Republicans believe that’s possible: by touting Trump’s closure of the border and hitting Democrats over the head with the culture war — while ignoring the drag his mass deportations have had on the region. The GOP faithful, clad in signature MAGA red and a few scattered Trump 2028 hats, gathered at a beer hall outdoors in 100-degree heat to greet the Republican Senate nominee and other candidates. Attendees ate up the Republicans’ constant jabs at Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico. Eric Flores, the challenger to Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, called Talarico a “gay vegan” and “low T.” Paxton belittled Talarico, a seminarian student and critic of Christian nationalism, for referring to himself as a “Christian who hates Christianity.” It’s an approach key to Paxton’s strategy, as Republican Senate nominee, to slice into Talarico’s widening polling lead with Hispanic voters, who could prove decisive for who wins the competitive Senate seat and a litany of other races that will determine which party takes power in Washington come November. “Once this community knows what [Talarico’s] views are on transitioning boys into girls, and girls into boys, and boys and girls sports, they're not going to support it,” Paxton told reporters after the rally, in response to a question of how he intends to keep Hispanic voters in the fold after they swung toward Trump in 2024. This has worked before for the Texas GOP. Sen. Ted Cruz blitzed the airways in the 2024 Senate race with attack ads against former Rep. Colin Allred about transgender youth participation in sports. Republicans branded Wendy Davis “ abortion Barbie ” following her successful protest against an anti-abortion law in the state legislature. But outside the carefully choreographed event is a community getting pummelled by the president’s increasingly unpopular immigration agenda — a reality that’s given Democrats a strong opening with Latinos as they attempt to end a decades-long losing streak in statewide races. Interviews with local lawmakers, business leaders and voters on both sides of the aisle reveal that Democratic candidates like Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa have so far been successful at appealing to Hispanic voters feeling the economic strain under Trump. Talarico, who appeared in McAllen for an event 16 hours after Paxton’s, kept his pitch focused on the cost of living, handing out hot plates of food and calling for a reversal in health care cuts under the GOP budget bill enacted last year. “He's pretty steady and focused on the issues that matter to families,” said Democratic state Sen. Juan Hinojosa, whose district spans Corpus Christi to McAllen. “Democrats get sidetracked on all these cultural issues, and they need to stay focused on what I call the bread butter issues, issues that impact families directly, the kitchen table issues,” he said. “Democrats need to stay away from biting the hook that's being put out by Paxton.” A community being squeezed The Rio Grande Valley is buckling under the weight of Trump’s policies, and the economic strain is visible in McAllen. Deportations have dried up workforces in critical industries like construction that drive the local economy, leaving cement slabs half-poured. A traffic chokehold at the border has slowed business in retail and restaurants as Mexicans have been deterred from hopping over to the U.S. for the day. The entire border is being squeezed. Laredo, located more than 150 miles from McAllen, is one of the nation’s top trade hubs, and its leaders are warning that Trump’s tariffs and his threat to eliminate the USMCA trade agreement stands to devastate international commerce that flows through the city. “When the U.S. doesn't provide economic opportunity for the people at the border, it will create this situation,” said Laredo Mayor Victor D. Treviño, a Democrat, in an interview. The Paxton campaign dismissed concerns of Democrats’ gains with Latinos, especially in the Rio Grande Valley — and once again emphasized the culture war, which Republicans say resonates with socially conservative Latinos. "Look, Hispanic families aren't voting for a woke vegan who says God is nonbinary and wants to Latinx our children,” said Alex Alarcon, director of Hispanic outreach for the Paxton campaign, in a statement. “We're proud of our culture and our faith, and Ken Paxton has spent his career fighting for us: a secure border to protect our families, a cost of living we can actually afford, and the freedom to live by our values.” Still, the tide seems to be turning toward Democrats. A dozen residents along the border said in interviews that they are satisfied illegal border crossings have dropped to record lows, a realization of one of Trump’s top campaign promises and one of the reasons he won over Hispanic voters in the region. But they also believe the crackdown has gone too far. More than 60 percent of Hispanics said Trump’s mass deportations campaign — including his widespread deployment of ICE agents across the U.S. — has been too aggressive, according to a July POLITICO Poll. In McAllen last week, the community was still aghast over a nun who was recently arrested by ICE while walking to church. She was later released after GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz and Democrat Rep. Henry Cuellar intervened, but interviews with residents revealed they still live in fear: Even U.S. citizens are checking their pockets for ID before venturing out, and they try to steer clear of the border if possible. Across Texas, one in five Hispanic business owners said they’ve had an employee deported in the past year and 70 percent have been impacted by Trump’s tariffs, according to a June survey commissioned by the U.S. Hispanic Business Council and shared first with POLITICO . Talarico holds a seven-point lead over Paxton among those surveyed — even though a plurality of them self-identified as Republican. A national Republican close to the race, granted anonymity to speak freely, countered that Paxton stands to benefit from some of the most competitive House races taking place in South Texas — where Republican Tano Tijerina and Flores are trying to oust Reps. Henry Cuellar and Gonzalez, respectively, and Rep. Monica De La Cruz is fending off a challenge from Tejano music star Bobby Pulido. GOP campaigns have stood up multiple field centers in those districts drawn to favor Republicans under a new Congressional map, a ground game that is expected to boost Paxton at the top of the ticket, the person said. They added that internal message testing shows some of the attacks on Talarico, specifically those regarding his past comments on gender, "is unlike anything we've ever seen with Hispanic men, just in terms of the amount that it moves them." Daniel Garza, president of the LIBRE Initiative, a grassroots conservative group based in South Texas, said Trump’s closure of the border has affirmed Hispanic’s support for him, and Democrats aren’t offering viable pro-growth economic plans. “Democrats have failed to give Latino voters something to vote for, and that they've only focused solely on something you know for us to vote against. And that's not good enough,” he said. “[Latinos] want less tax burden, less regulatory burden, more energy production.” Talarico’s pitch to Hispanics Talarico was also in McAllen, just one day after Paxon’s rally, to host a fundraising benefit — the final stop on a 750-mile bus tour hitting small towns along the border to deliver a message about lowering costs and creating jobs. In an attempt to cast himself as a tough-on-immigration Democrat, Talarico unveiled a border security plan that includes hiring more Border Patrol agents, a major employer in South Texas, and adding immigration judges to reduce the asylum backlog. It’s part of his attempt to widen his current edge over Paxton with Hispanics, with a New York Times poll in June showing Talarico is winning the demographic by a 61 percent to 29 percent margin — a significant shift after Trump won 55 percent of Hispanic voters in Texas in 2024. “You could drive a truck through the margin of error on the Times’ subsample,” Alarcon, Paxton’s Hispanic outreach director, said. “The fact is nobody is winning Hispanic voters by default this cycle. We’ll be in Spanish-language media from the Valley to Dallas, talking about groceries, gas, health care and a secure border.” Still, Talarico’s lead has given Democratic party leaders hope amid their national tug-of-war with Republicans over Hispanic voters: If Talarico can hold onto Texas’ large Latino population by these margins through November, that would prove gradual gains over the past decade for Republicans were a temporary blip ahead of the 2028 presidential race. Under the midday sweltering sun in McAllen, Talarico handed out hot plates of food to a line of people who had donated to a local woman struggling to pay for cancer treatment. The Democratic Senate nominee, while speaking to reporters later, dismissed Paxton’s attempts to appeal to Hispanic voters by making personal attacks against him. Republicans are attempting to divide people, Talarico said, “so we don't notice that they're picking our pockets, that they're closing our public schools, that they're gutting our health care, that they're raising taxes on working people while they cut taxes for billionaires. It's the oldest strategy in the world.” Talarico’s campaign is leaning hard into its outreach to the Hispanic community, including efforts like running a Spanish-language ad during the World Cup talking about his background as a teacher, plans to defend Medicaid and social security, and push to raise taxes on billionaires. He also ran an ad during the Mexico vs. Panama soccer match and launched a Spanish-language social media channel. Local Democratic party officials have begun targeted organizing efforts to turn out Hispanic voters throughout the Rio Grande Valley. But the challenge, they say, is convincing Hispanics running away from Republicans to instead run toward Democrats and not stay home in November. Democrats are heartened by an uptick in primary turnout in the region, which in March saw more than double the number of primary voters than in 2024. Trump carried all four counties in the RGV that year, the first time in history a Republican has won them at the presidential level, but Democrats won at every level down ballot. “We're hoping to carry that momentum,” said Hidalgo County Democratic chair Richard Gonzales, referring to the high primary turnout. “Republicans beat us because they made it seem like they could solve the problems. They got in and then they just created more problems.”
articles.headline: In South Texas, Paxton tests the limits of Trump’s Hispanic coalition

articles.body: Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Rep. Haley Stevens in her state’s contentious Democratic Senate primary on Friday, wading into one of the highest-profile ideological battles within the Democratic Party. “As governor, I have one strategy: Get things done. And that strategy informs everything that I do, and that’s why I’m endorsing Haley Stevens for the U.S. Senate,” Whitmer said in a video posted to Stevens’ account . Stevens is hosting a meet-and-greet alongside the governor and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.) in Detroit Friday afternoon. Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed are the two major Democratic candidates competing in the Aug. 4 primary to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters. El-Sayed’s candidacy has galvanized progressives, while Stevens has backing from more mainstream Democrats and the tacit support of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. “I am absolutely thrilled to have Gov @GretchenWhitmer’s endorsement for U.S. Senate,” Stevens said in a post on social media . “She is a champion for our state, she understands the stakes of this race and why it’s so important we elect the strongest Dem in this primary, and she gets stuff done for Michigan. Let’s go win!” The race has gained national attention as Democrats aim to keep the seat blue and Republicans vie to flip the seat. Whoever wins the Democratic nomination will face GOP candidate and former Rep. Mike Rogers, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, in November. Stevens and El-Sayed represent the party’s ideological split, with Stevens representing the more moderate lane of the party and El-Sayed the progressive wing. That’s also evident in who endorsed them. Stevens received an additional endorsement from outgoing Sen. Gary Peters and El-Sayed has been endorsed by more progressive lawmakers such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.). In Warren’s endorsement video, she praised El-Sayed’s vow to not take corporate money while taking a jab at Stevens, who has benefitted from a slew of outside donations — including nearly $30 million from the AIPAC-aligned United Democracy Project.
articles.headline: Gretchen Whitmer endorses Haley Stevens for Michigan Senate seat

articles.body: Democrats voted to make South Carolina their first presidential primary state for 2028 — a significant shift from past election cycles, and one that prioritizes a state with a significant Black voting bloc. The Democratic National Committee’s Rules and Bylaws Committee on Friday scheduled the Palmetto State’s primary for Jan. 22 and tentatively set the rest of its early-voting calendar in a surprisingly tense voting session. It will be followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia. The decision to choose South Carolina over Nevada, another historic early state in contention for first place, came down in part to concerns about Nevada’s ability to process election results quickly. Democrats said they were also looking to strengthen Black voting power in the South after the Supreme Court significantly restricted the Voting Rights Act earlier this year, which triggered redistricting efforts. Michigan bested Iowa in the vote to be the Midwest’s early state — a notable departure, as Iowa led the calendar for decades through 2020. New Hampshire, which has gone second on the nominating calendar in most past cycles, got bumped back to third place. Then, things got tense. The committee voted to add Virginia and New Mexico to host early-state primaries for the first time. But Democrats also proposed having New Mexico vote on Feb. 15, before Michigan, because Democrats there can’t move their primary unilaterally. That’s a major departure from a monthslong, widely agreed upon plan from the DNC members to give one of the first four early states to the South, Northeast, West and Midwest. The adopted calendar leaves the Midwest, a crucial region for Democrats’ path to victory in 2028, represented fifth, and sparked frustration from a number of Midwestern members of the DNC. “We had four regions for a reason, and we should be respecting that,” Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) said during the meeting. “For too long, Democrats flew over the Midwest.” The proposed calendar will be voted on by the full DNC at its August meeting in Austin. The slate of early nominating states — and their specific order — will significantly shape the path to victory for the field of Democrats eyeing the 2028 presidential nomination. It elevates the South and Southwest, which boasts large populations of Black and Latino voters, and weakens the voices of Democrats from the Northeast and Midwest. And it happened partly by accident. Jane Kleeb, chair of the Nebraska Democratic Party, said the mid-September deadline to move a state’s primary date caught her and other members by surprise – and ultimately ended up costing Michigan an even more prominent placement. “The rule was passed last year. A lot of us, because we deal with a lot of things, just forgot about it,” Kleeb said. “We all thought we had until Jan. 15, which would have given more time to do it.” Dennis Speight, a DNC member from Texas who supported New Mexico getting moved into the early round of states, argued it would have gotten lost if it had been stuck between two larger states. “We wanted to do mostly smaller states first, and did not want New Mexico, which we spent a lot of time adding to the mix to get to that sixth state, to get lost in that shock,” Speight said after the vote. “If we had sandwiched New Mexico in between Michigan and Virginia, given their number of delegates, New Mexico might have gotten lost.” DNC chair Ken Martin, who previously led the Minnesota Democratic Party, said he believes Michigan will still play a big role in selecting the next nominee. “As a proud Midwesterner, I want to make sure that Michigan does not get overlooked,” Martin said after the meeting. “When you think of all the other states and the number of delegates that will come out of Michigan and Virginia compared to the other states, there's no way they're going to be overlooked in that process.” And Dingell said after the vote that Michigan’s role as the first large state on the calendar would prevent it from being overshadowed, adding that presidential candidates “are going to be there, they’re going to have to talk about the issues.” Friday’s vote was the culmination of months of intense lobbying by some of the top politicians and operatives across the nation’s battlegrounds, a furious effort that played out in public letters and over private drinks and included handwritten notes from New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham and literal sweeteners in swag bags of local goods. South Carolina and Nevada, which in recent years had been third and fourth in the process, emerged as frontrunners as Democrats who’ve long bemoaned the lack of diversity in Iowa and New Hampshire looked for ways to make increased overtures to Black and Latino voters. That desire only grew in the wake of the Supreme Court’s Callais ruling — and prompted Virginia to elevate a second southern state into the early window. Some Democrats additionally pointed to South Carolina’s role in propelling former President Joe Biden to the nomination in 2020. Biden won the state resoundingly, boosting his then-floundering campaign after underwhelming performances in Iowa and New Hampshire, before racking up huge victories across the Black-heavy South on Super Tuesday that launched him to victory. “They saved our entire country from Donald Trump,” said Kleeb. "They didn't just do it in 2020. They've done it over and over and over again." "Our party must acknowledge this now with actions," she continued. A number of potential 2028ers have already visited South Carolina well in advance of the DNC’s meetings. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), and former ambassador Rahm Emanuel have all traveled to the state this year. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) visited the state last summer. Nevada, a union-heavy battleground state with a diverse electorate and large Latino population, argued it was better positioned for the leadoff spot than reliably red South Carolina — a push backed by the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and Xavier Becerra, who is running to be the first Latino governor of neighboring California. But some RBC members worried Nevada’s grace period for counting late-arriving mail ballots could delay results and inject chaos into the nominating process from the jump if it was the first state. New Hampshire and Iowa Democrats decried the proposed calendar, which overturns their premium positions from past cycles. “The Democratic National Committee’s decision today is wrong for Democrats, wrong for New Hampshire, and wrong for the country,” said New Hampshire Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Maggie Hassan, and Reps. Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander in a statement. "This is just another example that National Democrats are truly out of touch with voters. Iowa is the center of the political universe right now," Iowa Democratic Party chair Rita Hart said. The DNC unsuccessfully attempted to add Georgia to its early window in 2024. Peach State Democrats were candid that their ability to fill a top slot would hinge on whether they were able to flip the governor’s and secretary of state’s offices in November — a gamble RBC members seemed unwilling to make. North Carolina also faced logistical hurdles.
articles.headline: Dems pick South Carolina to lead 2028 primary calendar

articles.body: Gas prices are high. Americans think they’re even higher. Three in five Americans believe gas prices in their area have risen by more than they actually have, according to an analysis of new results from The POLITICO Poll . It’s those perceptions that candidates will be running against this fall. Voters’ anxieties about fuel prices could give Democrats a boost ahead of the midterms, further strengthening the Democratic voting base and putting strains on the MAGA coalition as the increasingly unpopular war in Iran drags on. A plurality of Americans — 46 percent — say the change in gas prices will impact how they plan to vote come November. Most voters overestimated the change in gas prices in their area, according to the analysis of polling and granular pricing data provided by OPIS, a Dow Jones company that tracks gas prices. That includes majorities of voters who supported President Donald Trump and also those who supported former Vice President Kamala Harris. Roughly one in four Americans say gas in their local area has risen by $3.00 or more. But no zip code has actually seen that degree of change on average in the year and a half since Trump took office, as of early July. Frustrations over cost of living could be reinforcing existing negative views of the Trump administration: Harris voters are far more likely to overshoot the cost jumps than Trump voters, making it harder for Republicans to peel off Democratic voters. And the analysis shows a fracture among Trump voters. Self-identified MAGA Republicans were more likely to underestimate cost increases than non-MAGA Republicans — another crack in the president’s winning coalition as Republicans scramble to hold it together for the midterms. “It is a particularly tough dance that many Republican candidates will have to endure for the next three months,” said Arizona GOP strategist Barrett Marson. “How do you feel the pain of your voters without feeling the wrath of Donald Trump?” What’s more, American’s perceptions do not quickly change even when prices do. The POLITICO Poll asked about gas prices in both May, when they were near their peak, and July, when they had dipped. The results were the same in both. “President Trump and his energy team anticipated these temporary market disruptions, communicated them openly to the American people, and implemented an aggressive plan to mitigate any impacts,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. “As the U.S. military degrades the terrorist Iranian regime’s ability to attack commercial vessels and disrupt the free flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices will plummet back to pre-conflict levels.” Gas prices could swing votes Americans’ frustrations with prices and the economy overall are changing how they say they will vote in the fall. Of the 46 percent of Americans who said gas prices will have an impact on their vote, just under 40 percent said they are considering voting for a different party than they normally would, including 49 percent of MAGA Republicans and 57 percent of non-MAGA Republicans. “Three quarters of the country is confronting higher gas prices and feeling it,” said longtime Democratic strategist Jesse Ferguson. “That leaves them ... very vulnerable to the economic pain and very vulnerable to the economic argument the Democrats are going to make.” To better understand public perception of gas prices, The POLITICO Poll asked Americans how the price of gas in their area had changed since Trump took office. Respondents could choose between buckets like “$1 to $2 higher per gallon,” “$1 to $2 lower per gallon,” or say prices had stayed roughly the same. More than three-fourths said gas prices in their area have gone up. Using OPIS data, POLITICO compared each respondent’s answer against the actual average cost of regular gas in their zip code during the first week Trump was in office and the week prior to the July poll, which was conducted by the independent polling organization Public First from July 12 to July 15. That comparison revealed the difference between the pain the American public is feeling and where actual gas prices stand — and, in particular, how that pain is expressed differently among Democrats and Republicans. Roughly 70 percent of Harris voters and 54 percent of Trump voters overestimated the increase in gas prices in their area, according to POLITICO’s analysis. “Democrats are highly motivated,” as a voting base, Marson said. “The longer the war goes on, probably the less motivated Republicans will be.” The perception of higher gas prices is linked to how people see the economy — and who they blame for it. Across the country, 57 percent of Americans say the cost of living is worse than they “can ever remember it being.” Those who overestimate gas price increases had more than twice the odds of agreeing with that statement, even after controlling for demographics and their 2024 vote. Similarly, a plurality of Americans — 43 percent — blame Trump more than former President Joe Biden for the state of the economy overall. Those who overestimated their local increase in gas prices had nearly twice the odds of saying the same, compared with those who perceived the change in gas prices correctly or who underestimated the change. It's already affecting the battlegrounds In the country’s most competitive races, Republicans will have to answer for the perceived cost pressures of rising gas prices more often than Democrats. Thirteen of the most competitive districts have experienced gas price increases higher than the national average, according to POLITICO’s analysis. Of those, nine are currently represented by Republicans. In California’s 22nd District, where Republican incumbent Rep. David Valadao will face off against progressive political newcomer Randy Villegas, average prices across the district had gone up $1.17 by early July — the third highest increase of any district, according to POLITICO’s analysis. Villegas said in an interview that he thought frustration over gas prices would mobilize turnout in the fall, driven by how the cost of gas is “tied to every other thing.” “It’s the cost of gas when you’re driving to the grocery store, when you’re driving to, you know, see a doctor,” he said. Or, the cost of gas when driving 7 to 8 hours away to “go get cheaper health care.” Valadao did not respond to requests for comment. In Colorado’s 8th District, where gas prices have risen by $0.73 on average since Trump took office, Republican incumbent Rep. Gabe Evans blamed local Democratic policies for increased costs more than the Iran war. While “what's happening halfway around the globe has some impact on global energy prices,” Evans said, high gas prices in the district are “a direct result of the local economic policies — the anti-energy policies — of the state Democrats who run the state of Colorado.” But The POLITICO Poll results from this month show voters don’t necessarily feel the same. Roughly 63 percent of Americans selected “the war with Iran” as the primary reason why gas prices have increased since Trump took office, including 59 percent of Trump voters and 70 percent of Harris voters. By the middle of May, the average price of gas across the country reached its highest point of the Trump administration to date: $4.50 per gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In July, average prices dipped to $3.78 per gallon, the lowest average price since March. Still, in both months, more than 75 percent of Americans said gas prices had gone up, POLITICO’s polls show. And in both months, roughly 23 percent said prices had gone up by $3.00 or more. This week, Trump said the upcoming midterms would not impact how he goes about fighting the war with Iran. “I can't think about that having to do with this,” he said, referring to the elections. “I think people are very impressed.”
articles.headline: Poll: Republicans’ gas price problem is even worse than it seems

articles.body: <p>El magistrado José Luis Calama, instructor del <i>caso Plus Ultra</i>, da un nuevo paso en la investigación abierta contra el expresidente José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero. El juez ha decidido interrogar los próximos 7 y 8 de septiembre a Julio Martínez Sola, presidente de la aerolínea, y a su consejero delegado, Roberto Roselli, según reza una resolución fechada este viernes. Calama toma esta iniciativa después de que ambos <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-20/el-presidente-de-plus-ultra-implica-a-zapatero-en-el-cobro-de-una-comision-por-el-rescate-de-la-aerolinea.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-20/el-presidente-de-plus-ultra-implica-a-zapatero-en-el-cobro-de-una-comision-por-el-rescate-de-la-aerolinea.html">enviaran sendos escritos a la Audiencia Nacional</a> para implicar al exdirigente socialista en la obtención de ayudas públicas; en línea con el relato expuesto por Julio Martínez Martínez, dueño de la consultora Análisis Relevante, que señaló que el antiguo líder del PSOE “marcaba los pasos a seguir” en <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-21/el-empresario-julio-martinez-se-ratifica-ante-el-juez-al-senalar-a-zapatero-por-el-rescate-de-plus-ultra-pero-afirma-que-no-sabe-con-quien-hablo.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-21/el-empresario-julio-martinez-se-ratifica-ante-el-juez-al-senalar-a-zapatero-por-el-rescate-de-plus-ultra-pero-afirma-que-no-sabe-con-quien-hablo.html">las gestiones que desembocaron en el rescate de 53 millones de euros</a> que la compañía aérea recibió del Gobierno durante la pandemia de coronavirus.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-24/el-juez-calama-cita-a-declarar-a-los-directivos-de-plus-ultra-que-implicaron-a-zapatero-en-el-rescate.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El rey Felipe VI ha mostrado este viernes su preocupación por los incendios que en las últimas horas asolan numerosas zonas de España durante el encuentro que esta mañana ha mantenido con la presidenta del Gobierno de Baleares, Marga Prohens, en la ronda de audiencias a las principales autoridades políticas de Baleares que marcan anualmente el inicio de las vacaciones de la familia real en Mallorca. “El Rey sigue con preocupación y atención el tema de los incendios que se producen en todo el territorio, pero especialmente las últimas horas <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/el-gobierno-declara-la-emergencia-nacional-en-la-comunidad-de-madrid-y-en-avila-por-los-incendios.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/el-gobierno-declara-la-emergencia-nacional-en-la-comunidad-de-madrid-y-en-avila-por-los-incendios.html">de este fuego entre Madrid y Ávila</a>”, ha explicado la presidenta de Baleares, Marga Prohens, tras un encuentro de 45 minutos con el monarca. La líder del ejecutivo balear ha detallado que han hablado sobre la proximidad de las llamas a varios núcleos de población y sobre las características de la zona que, según Prohens, el Rey conoce “perfectamente”.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-24/la-preocupacion-del-rey-por-los-incendios-en-espana-centra-las-audiencias-a-las-autoridades-de-baleares.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El final del silencio de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero le ha servido al PSOE para mitigar parcialmente el desasosiego que le carcome desde hace más de dos meses. El Gobierno y el PSOE han cerrado filas formalmente y aseguran que probará su inocencia, pero el sabor de boca que el expresidente ha dejado en su entrevista en RTVE, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/zapatero-en-su-primera-entrevista-tras-su-imputacion-no-es-que-no-influyera-es-que-no-hable-con-nadie-del-rescate-de-plus-ultra.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/zapatero-en-su-primera-entrevista-tras-su-imputacion-no-es-que-no-influyera-es-que-no-hable-con-nadie-del-rescate-de-plus-ultra.html">en la que ha negado su participación en el rescate de 53 millones de euros de la aerolínea Plus Ultra</a> en la pandemia y no ha aclarado el origen de las joyas tasadas en 1,3 millones que guardaba en una caja fuerte en su oficina, empeora conforme se desciende en el escalafón socialista. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-24/las-explicaciones-de-zapatero-dejan-un-sabor-agridulce-en-el-psoe-a-pesar-del-cierre-de-filas-de-ferraz.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p><a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/jose-luis-rodriguez-zapatero/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/jose-luis-rodriguez-zapatero/">José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero</a> anunció, tras ser imputado por un presunto delito de tráfico de influencias y ser registrado su despacho el pasado 19 de mayo, que pronto iba a dar explicaciones a los ciudadanos. No lo hizo y cuando, el 17 de junio,<a href="https://elpais.com/videos/2026-06-17/zapatero-ya-ha-declarado-en-la-audiencia-nacional-que-viene-ahora.html#?rel=mas_sumario" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/videos/2026-06-17/zapatero-ya-ha-declarado-en-la-audiencia-nacional-que-viene-ahora.html#?rel=mas_sumario"> acudió a declarar ante el juez José Luis Calama </a>en la Audiencia Nacional, le pidió más tiempo —“una semana o diez días”— para aclarar el origen de las joyas que fueron halladas en una caja fuerte en su oficina de la calle Ferraz y tasadas, según un informe pericial, en 1,3 millones de euros. Pero tampoco lo hizo una vez expirado ese plazo. Este jueves, en <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/las-titulares-de-la-entrevista-a-zapatero-de-la-estrategia-de-defensa-de-julio-martinez-a-los-trabajos-de-sus-hijas.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/las-titulares-de-la-entrevista-a-zapatero-de-la-estrategia-de-defensa-de-julio-martinez-a-los-trabajos-de-sus-hijas.html">una entrevista en TVE,</a> es decir, más de dos meses después del hallazgo, cuando el periodista Javier Ruiz le preguntó de dónde habían salido, el expresidente del Gobierno se limitó a decir que eran <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/zapatero-rechaza-aclarar-el-origen-de-las-joyas-son-un-regalo-personal-de-cortesia.html" target="_blank" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/zapatero-rechaza-aclarar-el-origen-de-las-joyas-son-un-regalo-personal-de-cortesia.html">“un regalo de cortesía”,</a> pero continuó sin aclarar su origen. Eso lo hará, aseguró, ante el juez. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-24/implicaciones-politicas-eticas-y-penales-de-las-joyas-que-zapatero-asegura-haber-recibido-por-cortesia.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero sabe que tiene dos problemas. Lo ha dejado claro en su primera intervención pública tras conocerse su condición de investigado. El primer problema es con la justicia por estar inmerso en un proceso en el que defender su inocencia le demanda una estrategia jurídica sin margen para el error. Rodríguez Zapatero ha reclamado su derecho a la defensa y la presunción de inocencia apelando a la jurisprudencia del Tribunal Europeo de Derechos Humanos. También ha denunciado la violación de derechos sufrida al hacerse pública la totalidad de su agenda. El otro problema está conectado con el deber de explicación que se impone a quien ha ostentado la presidencia del Gobierno. ¿Cómo combinar esta estrategia sin comprometer la mejor defensa del ciudadano y la reputación del hombre público? La <a href="https://elpais.com/videos/2026-07-23/las-siete-claves-de-la-entrevista-de-jose-luis-rodriguez-zapatero-en-mananeros-en-video.html?autoplay=1" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/videos/2026-07-23/las-siete-claves-de-la-entrevista-de-jose-luis-rodriguez-zapatero-en-mananeros-en-video.html?autoplay=1">entrevista en TVE</a> ha sido la ocasión para intentarlo y esta encubría además un tercer objetivo todavía más exigente: contener los daños que <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/el-gobierno-y-el-psoe-cierran-filas-con-zapatero-y-aseguran-que-probara-su-inocencia.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-23/el-gobierno-y-el-psoe-cierran-filas-con-zapatero-y-aseguran-que-probara-su-inocencia.html">sobre el Gobierno</a> ha provocado la declaración de Julio Martínez atribuyéndole a Zapatero gestiones sobre el rescate de Plus Ultra. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-24/una-entrevista-tres-objetivos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

Bugada cap endins i eviteu acostar-vos a la vora de rius i rieres. Previsió horària per a Barcelona : 6 h: risc d’algun xàfec 9 h: ambient més respirable 12 h: domini del serè 15 h: calor a ratlla 18 h: s’esvaeix la xafogor 21 h: augment dels núvols També et pot interessar El radiosondatge de Barcelona revela com l’atmosfera perd el “tap” i es prepara per la pluja Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo 2 minuts de lectura Pluja localment intensa durant la matinada Es manté el temps insegur a l’entorn metropolità. Risc de xàfecs localment intensos a partir de la matinada i fins al matí de diumenge des del Tarragonès fins al Maresme. En concret, tot fa pensar que els primers nuclis de precipitació durant la nit podrien aparèixer a l’entorn de les dues o tres de la matinada cap al Tarragonès i Baix Penedès, tot just fregant la línia de la costa. Amb el pas de les hores i en acostar-nos a les primeres hores de diumenge, el risc de xàfecs podria concentrar-se a la vora de la ciutat de Barcelona, tanmateix amb un possible espectacle visual amb tempestes fortes mar endins . Existeix la possibilitat, doncs, que la pluja pugui descarregar de valent en algun municipi costaner, però alhora que, la part més intensa del canvi de temps acabi caient dins del mar. Ràpidament però, i a mesura que es faci de dia el vent de mestral escombrarà tots els núvols. Mig matí i migdia radiant i esplèndid , ara bé, amb un repunt del temps canviant i alguns ruixats durant la tarda, en principi més puntuals. Ambient més agradable Encara que de dissabte a diumenge la nit sigui feixuga, el canvi de masses d’aire ens durà un ambient clarament més respirable i confortable a partir del matí de diumenge. articles.body: Aquest dissabte molts ciutadans han notat una olor a cremat a Barcelona. Alguns han pensat que podia haver un incendi a la ciutat o al voltant, però la realitat és que ve de molt més lluny i de diversos indrets. Segons han comunicat els Bombers de la Generalitat, l’olor del fum d’incendis com el de la Sierra Oeste , a Madrid, o el de la Vall d’Uixó , a Castelló, ha arribat a Barcelona i també a altres punts de Catalunya. A la ciutat, es va viure una situació similar fa tres setmanes, quan l’incendi forestal de l’Aragó va fer que es notés aquesta olor a cremat a Barcelona i molts altres punts de Catalunya. Imatge de @zoom_earth on es pot veure el fum dels diversos incendis que afecten la península com el de #IFSierraOeste o #IFValldUixo . La dinàmica de vents a l'interior de la península fa que, en alguns punts de Catalunya, sigui perceptible. pic.twitter.com/qIZ8VwhFFf — Bombers (@bomberscat) July 25, 2026 Converses a les xarxes socials Arran d’aquesta pudor de cremar que s’ha sentit durant la tarda, diversos usuaris han destacat aquest fet a través de les xarxes socials. Han estat uns quants els missatges amb la pregunta, “fa olor de fum?” , i també han aparegut respostes d’altres usuaris confirmant-ho. articles.body: El barri Gòtic esdevé, un any més, l’epicentre de la fotografia experimental i, des d’aquest dimecres, acull la setena edició de d’ Experimental Photo Festival . La trobada internacional ofereix fins diumenge una vintena d’ exposicions, una setantena de tallers i una vintena de conferències per explorar noves maneres d’entendre aquest mitjà més enllà de la imatge digital amb el Centre Cívic Pati Llimona com epicentre. També et pot interessar Experimental Photo Festival 2026: programa Núria Dias 2 minuts de lectura Festival únic al món L’Experimental Photo Festival és l’únic festival del món que es dedica a la fotografia experimental. “La nostra intenció és reunir tots aquests artistes a Barcelona una vegada a l’any per trobar-se, compartir crear i ensenyar els seus processos”, explica Pablo Giori, codirector de l’Experimental Photo Festival. Enguany l’esdeveniment reuneix 300 artistes d’arreu del món. 21 exposicions de galeries internacionals El festival programa 21 exposicions gratuïtes en diversos espais del barri Gòtic com l’Espai Borsí o la Lab Nau Especial, amb propostes d’ artistes internacionals que exploren noves formes de crear imatges. Entre els treballs més singulars hi ha Flying Roots , de María Solaguren-Beascoa Negre , una exposició dedicada als ocells, especialment al trencalòs . L’artista ha dedicat 12 anys a fotografiar aquesta au dels Pirineus. Però no és una exposició de natura tradicional, és la primera del món feta amb la tècnica de la cianotípia tricromàtica ecològica . “He volgut imitar el canvi de color de les plomes del trencalòs amb el canvi de color de les fotografies”, explica l’artista. La fotografia en temps d’IA En plena era de la intel·ligència artificial i de la fotografia digital, el festival convida a repensar com es creen les imatges avui. Ho fa amb una programació que inclou 69 tallers per descobrir, o redescobrir, tècniques històriques i processos fotogràfics artesanals, com el de la canadenca Ella Morton , que aquesta tarda ha impartit un taller sobre intervenció en pel·lícula fotogràfica. La trobada també reuneix una vintena de conferències, com la de Justin Quinnell , expert a fotografiar eclipsis solars com el del pròxim 12 d’agost , que qüestiona la nostra necessitat de fotografiar-ho tot, o la d’aquells ponents que exploraran com conviuen avui els processos analògics amb les eines digitals. També et pot interessar El KBr exposa Minor White i Tusquets de Cabirol, dos renovadors de la imatge de principis del s. XX Mercè Alsina 2 minuts de lectura

articles.body: Les festes de Gràcia són una de les festes majors més grans de l’estiu, i també de l’any, a Barcelona. Ja es coneixen les novetats d’enguany, se n’ha fet públic el cartell , obra de Pol Lupiáñez Ortega , i el pregoner , que serà Vicenç Sanclemente. articles.body: El Barça ja ha començat la pretemporada sota la batuta de Hansi Flick . Amb el tècnic alemany a la banqueta, l’equip ha guanyat les dues lligues disputades i ara buscaran la tercera, a més a més de l’assalt a la somiada Champions. Per intentar assolir-ho, necessitaran fer una bona pretemporada . Amb una estada a Anglaterra ja confirmada, el conjunt blaugrana ha fet oficial un triangular internacional a Udine davant l’Udinese i el Nottingham Forest. Tancarà la pretemporada el tradicional Trofeu Joan Gamper amb l’ Al Ahly com a rival. Partits a Anglaterra i Itàlia A diferència d’altres temporades, amb partits a països exòtics, aquest any la direcció esportiva ha escollit  Anglaterra i Itàlia com a destinacions. L’expedició blaugrana es desplaçarà a  Saint George’s Park del 27 de juliol al 3 d’agost , unes instal·lacions de referència del futbol anglès, seu habitual de les concentracions de la selecció anglesa i on ja hi va fer dues estades de pretemporada; una a l’estiu del 2014 i l’altra al del 2016.  Posteriorment, el 8 d’agost , als jugadors blaugrana els espera un triangular internacional a la Friuli Venezia Giulia Cup . Allà s’enfrontaran amb l’ Udinese Calcio , equip que milita a la Serie A, i amb el Nottingham Forest , de la Premier League. Al Ahly rival al Gamper El rival del Barça de cara a la 61ena edició del Trofeu Joan Gamper serà l’Al Ahly . El club egipci serà el primer club africà en jugar el torneig amistós del FC Barcelona. El partit es disputarà a l’Spotify Camp Nou el pròxim dimecres 19 d’agost , l’hora encara està per confirmar. El conjunt blaugrana i l’egipci s’han enfrontat en dues ocasions, el 2007 i el 2009, amb victòria per golejada dels catalans. articles.body: Els pericos somriuen il·lusionats després que Monchi hagi assegurat que “encara queda per acabar de completar la plantilla” i, que per tant, hi haurà nous fitxatges. Les pròximes setmanes, doncs, seran clau de cara a la confecció de la plantilla blanc-i-blava. Això sí, Monchi ha deixat clar que el club no té pressa per incorporar nous jugadors. “Perquè arribin jugadors s’ha d’alliberar espai i és la labor més difícil” , ha explicat, tot confirmant les sortides de Grajera i Salinas . El gadità, a més, defensa una política de fitxatges prudent: “Prefereixo portar jugadors dels que n’estic segur i no fitxar per fitxar” . A més, ha insistit en la importància de donar oportunitats al planter: “Hem de deixar que jugadors de baix pugin, i que el qui truqui la porta li puguem obrir” , ha explicat Monchi . També et pot interessar L’Espanyol ensopega amb el Sabadell en l’estrena a casa Redacció Esports 1 minut de lectura Monchi té clar quins són els objectius de l’Espanyol Més enllà del mercat, Monchi s’ha mostrat satisfet amb els seus primers mesos al club. “Estic content i feliç de com ha anat tot des que soc aquí, amb el club i amb el dia a dia de la feina” , i assegura que també està “satisfet de com m’està acollint l’afició perica” . De cara al futur, ha explicat que la pretemporada serveix perquè “el que entrenem surti al camp, i de moment està sent així” , però ha remarcat que el gran repte és “consolidar el projecte i forjar unes bases” . L’objectiu, segons ha dit, és “estabilitzar l’Espanyol en una zona tranquil·la de la classificació” , perquè si arriben moments difícils, “la caiguda no sigui excessivament dura” . Tot plegat, amb la voluntat de “seguir creixent i que les coses surtin bé” .
articles.headline: Monchi assegura que l’Espanyol continuarà actiu al mercat: “Encara hem de completar la plantilla”

articles.body: El globus meteorològic llançat aquest dissabte al migdia des del terrat de la Facultat de Físiques de la Universitat de Barcelona ha detectat que l’atmosfera ha perdut el “tap” que frenava el creixement dels núvols , respecte de les dades obtingudes de matinada, i ara és més favorable a la formació de tempestes . També et pot interessar L’altra cara de l’estiu: núvols i xàfecs arribaran aquest dissabte, 25 de juliol Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo 2 minuts de lectura L’atmosfera ja dona pistes Durant hores, l’atmosfera ha tingut energia acumulada però, alhora alguna cosa impedia que s’alliberés. Com una tapa invisible , una capa estable frenava l’ascens de l’aire calent i humit i dificultava el creixement dels núvols. Aquest migdia, però, aquesta barrera ha anat desapareixent . El radiosondatge de Barcelona ha detectat que l’atmosfera ha perdut aquest “tap” i ara presenta unes condicions molt més favorables per al desenvolupament de tempestes. També et pot interessar Quanta pluja ha caigut a Barcelona el 2026? Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo 1 minut de lectura El gran canvi: desapareix el “tap” atmosfèric a Barcelona Durant la matinada, el radiosondatge mostrava una atmosfera amb energia disponible, però amb una barrera que dificultava que aquesta energia s’alliberés. És el que coneixem amb el concepte de inhibició convectiva , una capa d’aire més estable que actua com un “tap” i impedeix que les bombolles d’aire calent de les capes baixes pugin amb facilitat. Aquesta matinada, l’instrument que analitza l’estructura vertical de l’atmosfera ha revelat que hi havia combustible, però el motor no podia arrencar , tot i tenir un ambient potencialment inestable . El radiosondatge de les 00 UTC (2 h de la matinada hora local) mostrava una situació curiosa: gran quantitat d’energia disponible per als corrents ascendents , una atmosfera inestable, valor alt que reforçava el potencial convectiu, aigua precipitable de 47 mm i, per tant, una columna atmosfèrica amb força contingut d’humitat . Però al mateix temps hi havia un element determinant. Malgrat tenir molta energia disponible, la convecció no s’activava fàcilment. Era com tenir una olla amb molta calor però amb la tapa posada . També et pot interessar Com s’explica que el radar, de vegades, no marqui la pluja que cau o al revés? Ariadna Corominas del Hoyo 3 minuts de lectura Dotze hores després, el radiosondatge de les 12 UTC ha mostrat una atmosfera diferent. Ara ja no hi ha una barrera energètica que dificulti l’ascens de l’aire . Al migdia, amb l’escalfament solar de la superfície, aquesta barrera s’ha anat debilitant fins a desaparèixer pràcticament. L’atmosfera ha quedat més “lliure” perquè l’aire calent i humit pugui ascendir. Els núvols tenen més facilitat per créixer També, un dels canvis importants que hi ha hagut és que, a partir d’aquest migdia, als núvols els costa menys arribar al punt on poden créixer per si mateixos . Ara, tenen més facilitat per créixer. D’altra banda, però, tot i que la columna atmosfèrica ha perdut humitat disponible, això no vol dir necessàriament menys potencial de tempesta: la humitat és només una peça del trencaclosques. I és que, el radiosondatge no diu exactament on plourà, però sí respon una pregunta clau: l’atmosfera està preparada perquè una tempesta pugui desenvolupar-se? Ara ja sabem que, a partir del migdia l’atmosfera al damunt de la vertical de Barcelona està més ben preparada perquè els corrents ascendents pugin alimentar els núvols de tempesta . nou canal de WhatsApp Vols rebre cada dia la previsió del temps per WhatsApp?
